profile.reading:
At 601 Benjamin Drive in Springfield, Ohio, LexisNexis operates a data center that the company itself has described in unusual technical detail -- not through marketing material, but through an exhibit filed in litigation. That filing puts the facility at 62,000 square feet, split roughly into 20,000 square feet of raised-floor data storage space, 20,000 square feet of office space, and 18,000 square feet of mechanical and electrical plant supporting the rest of the building. On the power side, the exhibit describes three 2-megawatt diesel generators synchronized to each electrical bus, for a stated 6 megawatts of standby generation capacity -- a figure that reflects the site's backup generation rather than an independently confirmed critical IT load, since generator nameplate capacity and actual continuous computing load are not the same measurement.

LexisNexis is the legal, regulatory, and business-information subsidiary of RELX, best known for its Lexis and Nexis research databases used by law firms, courts, and corporate legal departments across the country. A facility of this kind -- combining raised-floor computing space with a substantial mechanical and electrical plant and standby generation -- fits the profile of a company-operated data center supporting LexisNexis's own information-services infrastructure rather than a colocation facility marketed to outside tenants. Springfield, Ohio, roughly 25 miles northeast of Dayton, has been home to LexisNexis operations for decades, reflecting the company's historical roots in Dayton-area legal publishing going back to the Mead Data Central era.

Because the available public detail comes from a litigation exhibit rather than company marketing, it is narrower than a press release would be: it establishes the building's footprint, its internal space allocation, and its generator-based backup power arrangement, but does not address cooling technology, redundancy tier, network connectivity, or current utilization. No additional permit, zoning, or news coverage specific to this address was found to supplement or contradict those figures. What the record shows is consistent with a mature, established regional data center supporting a legal-information company's ongoing operations rather than a recently built or actively expanding facility. LexisNexis operates as part of RELX (formerly Reed Elsevier), a London-headquartered information and analytics group whose businesses span legal research, scientific and medical publishing (through its Elsevier division), risk and fraud-analytics services, and business events. The Lexis and Nexis databases that give the Springfield-area operation its name are used across the US legal system by law firms, courts, and corporate counsel for case law research, regulatory tracking, and public-records searches, which makes reliable, well-backed-up computing infrastructure directly relevant to the company's core product rather than incidental to it. That the clearest public description of this particular building comes from a court filing rather than company marketing is a reminder that not every data center's technical profile is meant for public consumption -- companies whose core business is neither hosting nor colocation typically have little incentive to publish facility specifications, and this one only became visible because a legal dispute required disclosing it.

reading.body:
The LexisNexis Springfield facility in Ohio publishes 6 megawatts of power capacity, derived from three synchronized 2 megawatt diesel generators. At typical AI training density of 40 kilowatts per rack, this amount of power could support roughly 150 racks, though the facility's actual IT load and use case are not published. The 62,000 square feet comprises 20,000 square feet of raised floor data storage, 20,000 square feet of office space, and 18,000 square feet of mechanical and electrical plant.

This facility ranks fifth among the eight facilities in Ohio with published megawatt figures. Ohio's mapped data center footprint includes 76 facilities total, of which only eight have disclosed capacity. The state's published capacity sums to 60.4 megawatts, meaning this single facility represents roughly 10 percent of Ohio's disclosed data center power.

LexisNexis operates this facility as internal infrastructure rather than a public cloud campus. The published capacity comes from a litigation exhibit and reflects generator nameplate rather than measured IT load. Without disclosure of actual tenant workloads or utilization, the facility's relevance to AI scaling cannot be determined from available facts.
